articles.title: Seahawks-Raiders Wednesday injury report: Leonard Williams still out, Rashid Shaheed returns
articles.summary: Early indications suggest that the Seahawks will limp into the game for the second week in a row.
articles.body:
The Seattle Seahawks emerged victorious in an injury bowl against the Arizona Cardinals last week, and it appears they may have to do it again on Sunday against the Las Vegas Raiders.

Seattle released the first of the three weekly injury reports, which is headlined by the health of backup quarterback Drew Lock, who is battling a lingering elbow injury and a new oblique injury. Lock was limited in practice on Wednesday, with head coach Mike Macdonald indicating that the veteran is "making good progress" and may start against the Raiders.

The ominous messaging leaves the entirety of Seattle on Jalen Milroe watch yet again as the second-year player is the only other healthy quarterback on the Seahawks' 53-man roster and would come in if Lock couldn't play.

Whoever is under center will once again be working with a patchwork offensive line as stars Quenton Nelson and Charles Cross did not practice. Nelson is battling a knee injury that might hold him out for his second straight game while Cross has been out with an ankle injury since Week 7. Backup guard Anthony Bradford continues to be hampered by a knee injury and was limited on Wednesday.

The Seahawks offense appears to have a weapon returning as wide receiver and kicker returner Rashid Shaheed was a full participant in practice. Shaheed has had a quiet 2026, but remains a key piece to unlocking the Seahawks' offense as the organization is hopeful he emerges as a second option beside Jaxon Smith-Njigba.

On the defensive side, Leonard Williams remains out with a stinger that he suffered against the Kansas City Chiefs, and edge rusher Derick Hall was limited with a new back injury. Both would be a massive loss for the Seahawks front that will hope to ruin Raiders' rookie Fernando Mendoza's debut.

It wasn't all negative for the Seahawks' defense, though, as signs are trending positive for edge rusher Uchenna Nwosu, who was limited with the ankle injury that's held him out of the team's last two games.

Meanwhile, the Raiders report was considerably smaller, so it appears they'll be near full-go against their former AFC West rival. For the Seahawks, they will have two more days of practice before setting game designations, so here's to hoping that the report shrinks throughout the week.

Sandfort has picked up right where he left off last season, as the senior is averaging 22.5 points, 3.0 rebounds and 3.0 assists and 2.0 steals per game while shooting 59 percent from the field. He has three straight 20-point efforts dating back to last season's NCAA Tournament.

Nebraska shouldn't have that much trouble with Lindenwood.

The Huskers enter the week ranked 25th in the polls. That should hopefully climb here in the next couple of weeks. Hopefully Braden Frager shoots better from deep. articles.title: Missouri State soccer eliminated from American tournament, awaits postseason bid
articles.summary: Missouri State men's soccer fell to Charlotte in the American Conference semifinals and awaits news on an NCAA tournament at-large bid on Monday.
articles.body:
No. 16 Missouri State soccer couldn't find the back of the net on Wednesday, Nov. 11. The Bears lost 3-0 to Charlotte in the semifinals of the American Conference Tournament in Tulsa, Oklahoma.

Missouri State (12-2-3) was scoreless with the 49ers at halftime. Charlotte was able to put together three impressive goals to send the Bears packing.

Charlotte opened the scoring with a goal in the 53rd minute. It was followed by a strong spell of play from the Bears and an equalizer looked likely, but Charlotte's defense cut down on angles and forced errant shots throughout the stretch.

See top photos from No. 12 Missouri State's draw with No. 16 Kansas City

The 49ers doubled their lead in the 80th minute behind a thumping strike from Michael Raggett for his 12th goal of the year. Charlotte put the game to bed in the 84th minute with a top corner goal from Xavier Halloway.

Missouri State finished with eight shots, four on target. It was the Bears' first game in 10 days after they received a first-round bye. They defeated Charlotte 4-2 on the road to close the regular season on Nov. 1.

Missouri State will await news of an NCAA Tournament bid on Monday, Nov. 16. The Bears will be confident they can snag a spot in the postseason tournament after spending most of the season in the top 25 in the national polls. There are 25 at-large bids in the 48-team postseason tournament.

The Bears currently have an RPI of 23 and have held a top 25 RPI throughout the year.

The American Conference hasn't sent an at-large bid to the tournament since 2023. The league had three teams qualify for the tournament that year.

The selection show will begin at noon on Monday. The first round of the NCAA Tournament will be played on Thursday, Nov. 19.

articles.title: Madison blanks Pompton Lakes for second straight field hockey title
articles.summary: Fueled by two first-half goals, Madison field hockey added to its storied history with a win over Pompton Lakes.
articles.body:
POMPTON LAKES − Madison needed less than 60 minutes to accomplish what 19 other teams failed to do over Pompton Lakes' first 23 games of the season.

Fueled by two first-half goals from sophomore Summer Graziano and a dominant defense performance, the Dodgers shut out Pompton Lakes, 4-0 in the North, Group 1 final on Nov. 11 at Lakeside Middle School, repeating as sectional champions and securing the 18th sectional crown in program history.

The result was even more impressive considering Pompton Lakes (19-3-2) had allowed just four goals all season entering the championship match. Madison (18-6) matched that total in a single afternoon while becoming just the third team to shut out the Cardinals this fall.

"It was so important for us to get those early goals. It's a big win for us, especially coming back from the hard loss in the [Morris] county final," Graziano said. "It's big for our team and our seniors who really want to go all the way. Now we get to continue to play in the states, which is a lot of fun."

Graziano put Madison in front with 4:45 remaining in the first quarter, then struck again just over four minutes into the second quarter to double the Dodgers' advantage to 2-0.

"If we came out ready to go and came out and scored first, we would be able to keep that momentum going rather than just playing from behind," Madison coach Sarah Morano said. "We wanted to do well and we wanted to get back here [sectional final]. We work hard every day to make sure that we pack our schedule against top 20 teams so that when we're in this situation we are ready to go."

Coming out of halftime, senior forward Celia Stuart found the back of the cage less than three minutes into the third quarter off a corner, giving Madison a 3-0 advantage.

Madison continued to capitalize on set pieces in the fourth quarter as Lindsay Cathpole scored off a corner with 8:20 left to complete the scoring. It marked the Dodgers' third goal generated from a corner and stretched the lead to 4-0.

"This is so much fun. I feel confident we'll go even farther this year and next year," Graziano said. "We have a great team and a good community. I think that really helps us."

The victory sends Madison to the Group 1 state championship game on Saturday, Nov. 14, where it will face South Jersey champion West Deptford at Bordentown High School.

articles.title: Jacoby Brissett's steady voice draws praise from Ravens' Cam Jurgens
articles.summary: Ravens center Cam Jurgens says veteran quarterback Jacoby Brissett brings needed leadership and stability to the team.
articles.body:
The Baltimore Ravens hope the addition of Jacoby Brissett can spark an offense that has gone through plenty of changes at quarterback. While Brissett is expected to take over as the starter, his impact could extend beyond the field.

Center Cam Jurgens is looking forward to having the 11-year veteran in the locker room and believes his experience playing in different systems will be valuable for the entire offense.

When asked what he has seen from Brissett during their brief time together and what the veteran can provide, Jurgens pointed to his leadership and communication.

"I mean, man, [Jacoby Brissett]'s a vet. He's been around a long time. He's been in about every system, played with a lot of guys, and he knows what looks right and what looks wrong. And honestly, I'm just excited to see his leadership coming in, his communication, how he talks with the guys, whether in practice or in the hallway, in meetings. [I'm] excited to learn from him too."

Brissett's experience could be especially important for a group that has dealt with changes at quarterback and center. Jurgens believes having someone who has been through different offensive systems can help provide some stability.

When asked what Brissett could offer the younger quarterbacks, Jurgens explained why communication will be so important moving forward.

"Just like I'm saying, [Jacoby Brissett]'s been around so many systems and teams. He knows what's good and what's wrong and how to fix things. Communication is always key when you're going through a lot of change. There's been a lot of different centers. There's been different quarterbacks, and so it's nice to have him in here and be a good steady voice for us."

Jurgens' assessment gives a player's perspective on the qualities Minter emphasized after the trade. Baltimore needs a quarterback who can communicate the assignment, recognize when something needs to change and keep the offense operating on schedule. Brissett's experience offers a foundation for that work, but the Ravens still have to develop the timing and shared understanding that come from practicing and playing together.

Defensive lineman Nnamdi Madubuike also believes Brissett's arrival has brought excitement to the locker room. Madubuike described the quarterback as a savvy veteran who can help the team get back to playing at a high level.

Monday will provide the first game evidence of how that preparation is translating. The encouraging signs Jurgens described are about Brissett's approach, rather than proof that Baltimore's offensive problems have been solved. Sustaining possessions, avoiding preventable mistakes, and getting the ball to the available playmakers will give the Ravens a clearer measure of whether the veteran presence is producing the stability they need.

The Ravens need more consistency on offense, and Brissett's experience gives them another voice who can help guide the group through a challenging stretch. Now the focus shifts to building chemistry and turning that excitement into better performances on the field.
authors: Steve Rudden and Glenn Erby , Ravens Wire

articles.summary: Ball State and Buffalo football's MACtion game is in a lightning delay. Here's what we know right now.
articles.body:
MUNCIE - Ball State football's second midweek MACtion game has been delayed.

The Mid-American Conference battle between Buffalo (6-3, 4-1 MAC) and Ball State (3-6, 2-3 MAC) was delayed about 25 minutes before kickoff due to lightning detected within an eight-mile radius of Ball State's Scheumann Stadium. The delay kicked in at 7:10 p.m. ET, about 25 minutes before the planned 7:35 p.m. Kickoff time.

The teams now plan to kick off at 7:45 p.m. ET, although the timer will reset if any more lightning is detected in the area. NCAA rules dictate that a 30-minute delay must be implemented when lightning is detected in the area. That timer resets with every new lightning strike.

Ball State is coming off a tough overtime loss at Umass last week, while Buffalo is looking to keep its chances at a MAC Championship berth afloat with a win over the Cardinals. This game marks the first return trip to Muncie for Buffalo head coach Pete Lembo, who previously served as Ball State's head coach from 2011-15.

This story will be updated if more delays occur.

articles.title: Bucs Week 9 snap counts reveal changes at receiver and safety
articles.summary: Tampa Bay's Week 9 snap counts reveal a major receiver shakeup, increased playing time for Bucky Irving and changes at safety.
articles.body:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers made noticeable offensive personnel adjustments in Sunday's 27-24 loss to the Chicago Bears , with rookie wide receiver Ted Hurst III nearly disappearing from the rotation as Tez Johnson took on a much larger role.

According to the official NFL gamebook , Tampa Bay played 68 offensive snaps and 61 defensive snaps. The participation totals reveal how the Buccaneers distributed playing time following Emeka Egbuka's return, while also showing a heavier workload for Bucky Irving and changes in the secondary after Antoine Winfield Jr. suffered an injury.

Ted Hurst III plays one snap as Tez Johnson takes larger role

Hurst's reduction in playing time was the most dramatic development among Tampa Bay's offensive skill players. After playing 42% of the offensive snaps against Atlanta in Week 8, the rookie appeared on just one of 68 plays against Chicago, accounting for 1% of the offense.

He got one target without a reception, and the Buccaneers relied on a different combination of receivers for the rest of the game.

Chris Godwin led the position group with 62 snaps (91%), followed by Johnson with 54 (79%) and Egbuka with 52 (76%). Johnson's participation increased by 37 percentage points from the previous game, when he played 42% of the offensive snaps.

The extra playing time led to a meaningful contribution. Johnson caught two passes for a team-high 76 receiving yards, including a 58-yard completion from Baker Mayfield on Tampa Bay's opening second-half possession. That reception advanced the ball to Chicago's 2-yard line and helped set up Irving's first touchdown.

Egbuka returned after missing the previous two games and caught three passes for 38 yards on five targets. His availability gave Tampa Bay another established receiving option, but Johnson's increased involvement and Hurst's near-total absence suggest a bigger adjustment to the rotation than simply reinserting Egbuka.

The snap counts show who got the opportunities, but they don't explain the coaching staff's reasoning for reducing Hurst's role.

Bucky Irving handles larger share of backfield

Irving played 47 offensive snaps (69%), up 19 percentage points from his previous appearance. Kenny Gainwell played 26 snaps (38%), down 12 percentage points.

The two running backs combined for 73 player snaps across Tampa Bay's 68 offensive plays, indicating they shared the field on at least five snaps rather than operating exclusively as substitutes for one another.

Irving handled the majority of the rushing production, finishing with 20 carries for 97 yards and two touchdowns. He also caught four passes for 28 yards, giving him 125 yards from scrimmage.

His touchdowns came on two- and six-yard runs, with the second score helping Tampa Bay tie the game at 24 late in the fourth quarter after Mayfield's successful two-point conversion.

Gainwell remained productive in a complementary role despite his reduced playing time. He finished with five carries for 16 yards and three receptions for 60 yards, including a 44-yard completion on third-and-nine during the first quarter.

The distribution reflects Irving's larger share of the rushing workload without eliminating Gainwell's involvement as a receiving option.

Tight end Cade Otton played all 68 offensive snaps, joining Mayfield and Tampa Bay's five starting offensive linemen as the only offensive players to participate in every play.

Otton finished with four receptions for 25 yards on eight targets, making him one of Mayfield's most-targeted receivers despite the limited yardage.

The remaining tight ends played considerably smaller roles. Payne Durham appeared on 14 snaps (21%), Bauer Sharp played eight (12%), and Ko Kieft participated in one offensive snap.

Otton's full-game workload shows how heavily Tampa Bay relied on him, especially compared with the other tight ends' limited offensive participation.

Winfield's injury forces adjustment in secondary

The biggest defensive personnel change came after Winfield suffered an injury in the second quarter.

Winfield played 29 defensive snaps (48%) before leaving the game, while Ifeatu Melifonwu appeared on 30 snaps (49%). The official gamebook later listed Winfield as out, confirming his absence through the rest of the contest.

Tykee Smith played all 61 defensive snaps, as did cornerbacks Zyon McCollum and Jacob Parrish and linebacker Alex Anzalone.

Melifonwu's increased involvement became particularly important late in the game. Chicago completed a 38-yard pass to tight end Colston Loveland on its final possession, with Melifonwu credited as the defender. The completion moved the Bears into field-goal range before Cairo Santos made the winning kick.

The snap distribution shows how Tampa Bay adjusted after losing Winfield, although the participation totals alone cannot establish every coverage responsibility or substitution decision.

Josiah Trotter remains a defensive fixture

Rookie linebacker Josiah Trotter played 59 of Tampa Bay's 61 defensive snaps (97%), continuing to handle one of the defense's largest workloads.

Along the defensive front, Calijah Kancey led the interior rotation with 45 snaps (74%), followed closely by Vita Vea with 44 (72%).

Keionte Scott played 39 defensive snaps (64%), while rookie edge rusher Rueben Bain Jr. appeared on 35 (57%). Anthony Nelson contributed 31 snaps (51%), with David Walker and Al-Quadin Muhammad each playing 28 (46%).

The distribution matters because YaYa Diaby was inactive against Chicago, leaving Tampa Bay to manage its edge-rushing rotation without one of its regular contributors.

Bain remained involved on more than half of the defensive plays, while Nelson, Walker and Muhammad shared the remaining workload.

Tampa Bay's defense forced five turnovers, including four interceptions of Caleb Williams, but the Buccaneers couldn't turn those opportunities into a win.

The Week 9 participation figures reveal two different personnel developments. On offense, Tampa Bay concentrated its receiving snaps among Godwin, Johnson and Egbuka while giving Irving a larger share of the backfield. Defensively, Winfield's injury required a safety adjustment, with Melifonwu taking on more responsibility in a game ultimately decided by Chicago's final possession.

articles.title: Houston Texans safety Reed Blankenship ready to return from broken hand, concussion against Browns
articles.summary: Reed Blankenship was injured against Jacksonville and has missed two games but is ready to return against Cleveland.
articles.body:
Houston Texans safety Reed Blankenship says he's ready to play this weekend versus the Cleveland Browns after missing the past few weeks with a concussion and a broken hand.

Blankenship, who last suited up against the Jacksonville Jaguars in London last month, returned to practice Wednesday as a limited participant.

"You don't really realize how much you love it until you … step back from it for a couple weeks," Blankenship said. "I'm glad I got to spend time with my baby girl too, my wife. But at the end of the day, not going out there and doing what I love for these past couple weeks hurt a little bit."

The Texans signed Blankenship in the offseason to a three-year deal but his start to the season was a rocky one. The lone new player in the Houston starting defense, the unit underperformed in the first few weeks with the secondary in particular taking a step back compared to last year.

Despite missing two full games and part of the Jaguars contest, Blankenship is third on the Texans in tackles and one of four players with an interception.

Safety M.J. Stewart, who missed the start of the season with an injury of his own, has filled in for Blankenship as the starting safety alongside Calen Bullock.

This wasn't Blankenship's first concussion, he said. But his perspective this time around the injury this time is different because of the family and life he is building outside of football.

"When I didn't have a kid and a wife, it was different," Blankenship said. "I wanted to stay out there and tough it out, was very stupid. But now start thinking about longevity. You want to be a dad, a father. You wanna be present."

Blankenship said he didn't know when during the Jaguars game he injured his hand. He has a visible scar on the top of his hand, and will probably wear a splint in games.

The 27-year-old safety is a right-hander for everything so injuring his left hand would be the preferred option for having a broken hand. But it didn't mean it was easy.

"You don't realize how much you need it until it's gone. Well, not gone," Blankenship said to laughs. "You know, gone for a couple weeks."

Linebacker Jake Hummel and cornerback Jaylin Smith also returned to practice Wednesday. Hummel has been injured all regular season while Smith got placed on injured reserve after the Week 4 loss to the Dallas Cowboys.

Both have a 21-day window to be activated from injured reserve.

David Montgomery didn't practice as he continues to rehab from a groin injury.

"David Montgomery is still going through the process," Texans coach DeMeco Ryans said. "He's getting better. We're encouraged by his progress so far."

Rookie Keylan Rutledge also didn't practice Wednesday with what Ryans called a "stinger." The official injury report listed the injury as neck/shoulder.

Rutledge has started every game this year at left guard after being taken in the first round of the draft.

"We'll see how he progresses throughout the week," Ryans said.

articles.title: Cam Schlittler unanimously wins AL Cy Young Award
articles.summary: The emphatic rise of a new ace in the Bronx is capped off with the ultimate pitching honor.
articles.body:
490 days ago, a lanky, 6'7" rookie from Walpole, Massachusetts, by way of Northeastern University, set foot on a major league mound for the first time at Yankee Stadium. It came just over three years after he was unceremoniously drafted in the seventh round of the 2022 MLB Draft with a very inefficient delivery and a fastball sitting in the high-80s.

By the time he debuted in the major leagues, he was throwing 100 mph. Three months after his debut, he shoved his childhood team into a locker in Game 3 of the Wild Card Series with one of the best playoff starts in franchise history. And as an encore in 2026? He proceeded to put up one of the greatest pitching seasons in franchise history.

Cam Schlittler's incredible rise as the Yankees' ace of the present and future has been completed, as he was named the 2026 AL Cy Young Award winner on Wednesday night, doing so unanimously.

Schlittler was engaged in a heated race with Toronto's Dylan Cease for much of the season, but the veteran faded with injury and ineffectiveness down the stretch, while the 25-year-old Schlittler wound up leading the American League in pretty much everything that mattered.

He finished the season with a 14-6 record, a 1.95 ERA, 0.92 WHIP, 239 strikeouts in 196 innings, a 215 ERA+, 2.56 FIP, and 7.0 rWAR. His numbers are historic. He is the first pitcher in the Junior Circuit to have a sub-2 ERA in over 190 innings since 2000 Pedro Martinez. His ERA+ is a franchise record, surpassing the standard-bearer, 1978 Ron Guidry (208).

He is the seventh Cy Young Award winner in franchise history, joining the likes of Sparky Lyle , Whitey Ford, Ron Guidry, Bob Turley, Roger Clemens, and Gerrit Cole, as well as the third unanimous winner, joining 1978 Guidry and 2023 Cole.

In the final voting total , he blew Cease out of the water, 210 to 110, by virtue of the Blue Jays' ace receiving only 22 second-place votes. Parker Messick of the Guardians came in third, followed by the Rays' Drew Rasmussen and Boston's Sonny Gray.

articles.title: As competitor, QB Daniel Jones wasn’t happy to see Colts as recent major trade sellers
articles.summary: Colts QB Daniel Jones voiced his recent displeasure over the team’s recent trades, but understood, it’s outside the players’ control.
articles.body:
Indianapolis Colts starting quarterback Daniel Jones publicly voiced his disappointment that his struggling team was a recent major seller ahead of this past Tuesday's league-wide trade deadline, while acknowledging, at least in his eyes, that it outside the players' control ( via the Athletic's James Boyd ):

In fairness, as a competitor, it would be a tough pill to swallow as a starting quarterback, knowing that your already below average wide receiver room to whom you regularly throw the football to is now without two of its best wideouts: Keenan Allen and Josh Downs—who were traded to San Francisco and Kansas City respectively.

It looks like still rehabbing Colts top wideout Alec Pierce is not coming back to the football field anytime soon, and you also lost your perennial All-Pro left guard Quenton Nelson, who consistently helped keep you upright in pass protection, as he was traded to Seattle to help jumpstart the ongoing rebuild for Indianapolis.

That being said, it's not as though Jones and his teammates, including those who recently were traded, didn't share in culpability to what led to the team's recent fire sale.

The team currently sits at 2-7, and among their defeats, lost to a winless Tennessee Titans team at home. Their brutal loss led to their longtime general manager Chris Ballard being fired thereafter, and that was the first domino to fall regarding the recent sell-off.

Two weeks later, the Colts would go on to be blown out in Jacksonville, 42-7, and it was clear their season was definitively over—if it wasn't already, after that dreadful rock bottom showing.

The Colts have now lost 5 straight games in 2026.

Dating back to 2025, they've lost 14 of their last 14 regular season games.

In particular, after landing a 2-year, potential $100 million contract extension, Jones, who's coming off a torn Achilles, has struggled this season and provided the Colts well below average starting quarterback play in 2026.

He's completed 182 of 302 pass attempts (60.3%) for 1,722 total passing yards, 6 passing touchdowns, and 10 interceptions during 9 starts so far in the 2026 campaign.

It's not all Jones' fault offensively though.

Even before the recent wide receiver trades, this was one of the league's worst wide receiver rooms collectively without Pierce back. It now resembles closer to a 2nd-team preseason squad. His pass protection also hasn't been great, even when Nelson was here, as a number of once reliable o-linemen have since struggled in pass protection.

That being said, a starting quarterback is the league's most valuable position, and almost always, if you don't have a 'dude' there, who can consistently elevate his teammates, carry the offense for stretches, and make pivotal, even difficult winning plays late in games, the whole team will struggle—or at least reach its inevitable end.

articles.title: The champion Valkyries have a Juste Jocyte problem and no easy answers
articles.summary: Juste Jocyte did not hold back on her team.
articles.body:
It appears that the Golden State Valkyries' championship hangover has begun.

In an interview with Lithuanian media , Juste Jocyte, the team's first-ever draft pick in franchise history, shared her frustrations about her playing time with Golden State throughout the season and the lack of communication (and inconsistent messaging) regarding her minutes, leaving her future with the team in doubt. While the interview was conducted in Jocyte's home language, multiple Valkyries reporters have agreed on most of the general messaging from the reports published this weekend. The lingering question is to what degree did she basically ask for a trade.

ClutchPoints reporter Kenzo Fukuda was the first in the media space to flag the interview, and he confirmed the Lithuanian player's frustrations through an anonymous source "close to the situation," which mostly stemmed from constantly moving goalposts regarding what it would take for her to see the floor this season. Fukuda, as well as reporter Marisa Ingemi of the Valkyries Beat outlet that covers the team, both highlighted a timeline of comments from head coach Natalie Nakase that seemed to indicate an evolving message at best. Jocyte needed to rest and recover after playing in Europe. Then it was about specific matchups . Then Nakase needed Jocyte to become more of a point guard, which Jocyte thought was antithetical to her on-court strengths and was the most frustrating note to hear, per Fukuda's source. Then it was about her defense . This season, Jocyte only broke the double-digit mark in minutes in six of the 16 games she played in, and she made just two appearances in the postseason that lasted five minutes and five seconds in total - one blowout win and one blowout loss.

At this point, it's worth highlighting Jocyte's pedigree that led to her being the No. 5 pick in the 2025 WNBA Draft. At 14, she became the youngest player to debut in EuroLeague Women, the top competitive level on the European continent. She won the EuroCup in 2023 with Lyon at 17, alongside current Valkyries teammate Gabby Williams, and played in both legs of the final. She won the inaugural FIBA Women's EuroBasket Rising Star award last year. She has two Lithuanian basketball player of the year awards under her belt (2022, 2025) and, at 20, is younger than every women's college basketball prospect coming out of school. At first glance, it hardly stands to reason that a player like her would need to improve on so many different parts of her game.

It's no surprise for a team to have high expectations of development from a rookie, especially one drafted No. 5 overall, regardless of their prior experience. However, this might be about more than just getting a player to adapt to the league. Eric Apricot, the founder of Valkyrie Nation , broke down a notable change in the team's front office between 2025 and 2026. Read his analysis, but in short, Vanja Cernivec was the team's vice president of basketball operations entering their first season and reportedly guided an internationally focused drafting and recruitment strategy. Then she left for the Portland Fire, where the philosophy shifted to fit in more with Nakase's defense-first, strength-in-numbers approach. International players certainly had roles in the Nakase system, such as Cecilia Zandalasini and even Gabby Williams, if you want to consider that the Nevada-raised player plays internationally for France, but there was apparently no space for Jocyte (or Sixth Player of the Year Janelle Salaun , for that matter).

Regardless of whether she asked for a trade - depending on the interpretation, she either straight-up told Ohemaa Nyanin that she doesn't want to come back to Golden State or at least implied that, if her frayed relationship with her coach and organization doesn't improve, then she doesn't want to return - the team reportedly wants her back. Ingemi cited a league source who said that the Valkyries "do see her as a part of their future." On a recent podcast appearance, team owner Joe Lacob even said he understood where Jocyte was coming from.

"I kind of understand. She's competitive and would like to win and didn't play," Lacob said on "The TK Show " podcast during Tuesday's episode. "But you know, she's also only 20. We had a pretty great roster, very deep. I think she can be a very good player, and we'd really love to have her back. So, I think she will certainly earn a lot more playing time in the future. I can understand there are emotional moments in the moment. She didn't get to play as much as she wanted to, and that's understandable."

That brings us to the matter of whether the Valkyries will have much say in her future. There's a world where both player and team settle their differences, leading to a happy ending in Golden State. Another possibility is that they agree on a mutual breakup and explore trade opportunities, despite what the team has said through this moment.

Then there's the reality where these thoughts are more than just "emotional moments" and she just doesn't come back. Her current team, Spar Girona, is much closer to home, and she could just stay abroad on a suspended contract (something she did for the 2025 season as part of an agreement with the Valkyries). Her deal would expire, and the Valkyries would retain her rights, but next offseason begins three straight years of expansion drafts. Unless the Valkyries want to protect a disgruntled player, she could be one her way out of Golden State for free if another team scoops her up in those drafts.

For fans who followed the team this season and were at the championship parade, Jocyte's comments might come as a bit of a shock. The 20-year-old said all of the right things about putting her ego to the side for the good of the team, particularly through a championship run. At the parade itself, she was easily one of the most excited players at the party, running up and down the street to celebrate and spray fans with champagne.

But the champagne eventually evaporated from Embarcadero, and so too did the smiles with the Valkyries. Now the cold, calculating part of the professional sports business has kicked in, and it could very well turn those championship celebrations into a distant memory far quicker than anyone could have anticipated.
